articles.title: Building a Switch courtroom where AI can negotiate but can't consent
articles.excerpt: A creative lead wants someone's portrait in a promo. That person wants to contribute, but doesn't want their face used. An AI can suggest a compromise. Who gets to say yes? I'm Harshil, a B.Tech AI/ML…
articles.body: A creative lead wants someone's portrait in a promo. That person wants to contribute, but doesn't want their face used. An AI can suggest a compromise. Who gets to say yes? I'm Harshil, a B.Tech AI/ML student in Delhi. My teammates Daksh, Kartik and I built Delegates Courtroom for Flip the Switch (Track 2: Best Personal or Creative Workflow). Two AI advocates negotiate a storyboard, and the humans keep control of their own briefs and the final approval. The rule we built around: agents negotiate, humans sign. What Switch does, in plain words Switch Rooms gives people and agents one shared place to work. Agents join with their own identities, get requests, read the room's context and reply like teammates. The shared room log is the part that matters.

articles.title: Why Hindsight Needs Evidence Before Suggesting CI Fixes
articles.excerpt: Why Hindsight Needs Evidence Before Suggesting CI Fixes Two CI failures can display almost identical error messages and still have different root causes. One timeout might be caused by a slow network…
articles.body: Why Hindsight Needs Evidence Before Suggesting CI Fixes Two CI failures can display almost identical error messages and still have different root causes. One timeout might be caused by a slow network dependency. Another might be caused by shared test state. If an AI assistant sees the same error text and immediately recommends the same fix, it could send a developer in the wrong direction. That is why FlakeTrail does not treat debugging as simply generating an answer from a log. Its reasoning workflow considers the current failure alongside historical investigations retrieved through Hindsight. The goal is to give developers useful context: what was previously attempted, which approaches failed, which fixes were verified, and what still needs investigation.
articles.author: Suresh Sharma

articles.body: My First Switch Hackathon: Setting Up an AI-Powered Workspace Introduction For the Flip the Switch Hackathon, I decided to explore how an AI-powered workspace could help organise and manage creative tasks. articles.body: Twelve and a half million active users got a new terminal emulator this year, and most of them will never know. They did not download anything, and nobody asked them to switch. JetBrains moved the terminal inside IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, and the rest of its IDEs onto libghostty-vt, the terminal emulation library extracted from the Ghostty project, and the usage count in JetBrains' own reporting alone cleared 12.5 million recurring users before any of the other adopters were counted. The post reached the Hacker News front page within hours, and the number that matters in it is not a benchmark.

articles.title: Turn a GAN Beauty Demo Into a Release Decision: Build an Evidence Gate for Tencent RTC Beauty AR
articles.excerpt: A polished GAN beauty demo can create momentum—and an uncomfortable question for the engineers in the room: Who decides whether this is actually ready to ship? The model can generate an impressive eff…
articles.body: A polished GAN beauty demo can create momentum—and an uncomfortable question for the engineers in the room: Who decides whether this is actually ready to ship? The model can generate an impressive effect. It cannot decide whether the visual result is respectful, whether the extra workload is acceptable on your supported devices, or whether an incomplete test run should count as evidence. That uncertainty is not a sign that your role has become less relevant. It is a sign that the difficult work has moved. Instead of asking only whether the effect works, the team needs an explicit release contract covering performance, visual review, consent, failure behavior, and ownership.
articles.author: LunarDrift

articles.title: Can an MCP Server Actually Help Prevent AI Agents From Leaking Secrets?
articles.excerpt: I've been experimenting with MCP servers and AI coding agents while building an open-source project called StagedSec. One thing I've been thinking about is where security checks should happen when an…
articles.body: I've been experimenting with MCP servers and AI coding agents while building an open-source project called StagedSec. One thing I've been thinking about is where security checks should happen when an AI agent works with a developer's repository. Most secret scanners operate on files, Git history, or commits. These are useful, but with AI agents, there's another interesting point: the moment an agent attempts to write something. Imagine an agent generating a configuration file containing: API_KEY=sk_live_... DATABASE_PASSWORD=... A scanner can find these values later, but what if we could inspect the content before allowing the write? That's one of the ideas behind StagedSec. What I'm experimenting with StagedSec currently has: A Go-based secret detection engine.
articles.author: intothewild

articles.title: Designing an AI incident agent for 3 a.m.: making memory visible
articles.excerpt: Picture the person who uses an incident tool. It's the middle of the night. An alert just woke them up. Customers are affected, a manager is asking for updates, and they are trying to read logs with h…
articles.body: Picture the person who uses an incident tool. It's the middle of the night. An alert just woke them up. Customers are affected, a manager is asking for updates, and they are trying to read logs with half-open eyes. That person doesn't need a clever chatbot. They need an answer they can trust in seconds, and proof they can check. Our team built DejaVu , an AI on-call agent that remembers how past outages were fixed. This post is about the design side: how we made an invisible thing, memory, visible and useful. The engine underneath DejaVu's memory is powered by Hindsight , an open-source agent memory system by Vectorize. Every past incident is stored in Hindsight.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission, the first Mars mission in 20 years. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected.

articles.title: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission
articles.excerpt: NASA is asking the public to send their names to Titan for an ambitious mission that will see a flying craft explore the Saturn moon in 2034, if all goes according to plan.
articles.body: We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034.

articles.title: SpaceX launches mystery mission for US Space Force in gorgeous sunset liftoff from California (video, photos)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California this evening (Nov. 6). It was the company's 125th liftoff of 2026.
articles.body: SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific. The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force , which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Nov. 6, 2026.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.title: AST SpaceMobile announces new 'Blacklift' rocket, targets 2028 launch debut
articles.excerpt: AST SpaceMobile plans to launch its broadband satellites on a new rocket called Blacklift, which it will build in house and plans to start flying in 2028.
articles.body: Another new private rocket is in the works. AST SpaceMobile announced today (Nov. 6) that it's building a reusable rocket called Blacklift to launch its broadband satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO), with first flight targeted in 2028. The news comes just 10 days after Cowboy Space unveiled Big Iron , a rocket designed to launch its constellation of 20,000 AI data centers . Cowboy Space is also targeting 2028 for its first liftoff. "The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry," Abel Avellan, the company's founder, chairman and CEO, said in a statement today .
